Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of how growth mindset, performance-avoidance goals, and responses to failure relate within Carol Dweck's framework:

## The Core Mindset Distinction

Carol Dweck's theory rests on a fundamental distinction about beliefs regarding ability. People with fixed mindsets believe that their talents, abilities, and qualities are carved in stone, whereas people with growth mindsets believe that their basic qualities such as talents and intelligence can be cultivated through their efforts (Dweck, 2006).

These contrasting beliefs shape behavior in profound ways. Those with fixed mindsets avoid challenges, give up when obstacles get in their way, ignore criticism, and find the success of others threatening. Those with growth mindsets embrace challenges, persist through obstacles, learn from criticism, and are inspired by the success of others.

## Response to Failure and Setbacks

The two mindsets produce strikingly different reactions to failure. The mindset framework summarizes research on how people think, feel, and respond to failure and challenging experiences. Individuals who believe that intelligence and ability are largely immutable ('fixed mindset') respond to failure by withdrawing, disengaging, or persisting with the same set of strategies despite their prior demonstrated ineffectiveness.

This research has deep historical roots. More than 30 years ago, Carol Dweck and her colleagues began studying student responses to failure, focusing specifically on why some students rebounded easily while others did not.

Dweck's early work identified two distinct behavioral patterns. Early efforts to understand how children respond to a challenge revealed two patterns of performance: mastery-oriented and helpless responses (Dweck & Leggett, 1988). The helpless response is characterized by avoidance of challenges and difficulty facing obstacles. In contrast, the mastery-oriented pattern involves seeking challenging tasks and persistence after failure.

By contrast, those with a growth mindset reframe failure entirely. As Dweck writes, "in the growth mindset, failure can be a painful experience. But it doesn't define you. It's a problem to be faced, dealt with, and learned from."

## Achievement Goals: Performance vs. Mastery

To explain these behavioral patterns, Dweck and colleagues turned to the concept of achievement goals. Seeking to explain these patterns, Dweck and colleagues posited that there may be a difference in achievement goals underlying the observed behavior (Elliot & Dweck, 1988). Some students see achievement situations as a test of their ability (i.e., performance goals), while others see them as learning opportunities which may increase their ability or understanding (i.e., mastery or learning goals) (Elliott & Dweck, 1988).

These goal orientations connect directly to mindset. When students have a growth mindset, they are more likely to focus on improving their malleable ability (i.e., mastery goals), while students with a fixed mindset are more likely to focus on demonstrating or hiding their fixed ability (i.e., performance goals).

The behavioral outcomes diverge accordingly. Students with mastery goals tend to confront challenge, show more effort, optimism, and effective strategizing (Elliott & Dweck, 1988).

## Performance-Avoidance Goals Specifically

Performance goals can be subdivided, which is key to understanding the relationship to failure. According to the trichotomous approach to achievement goals, performance goals can be further divided into performance-approach and performance-avoidance goals based on competence valence (i.e., competence beliefs such as self-efficacy). Performance-approach goals focus on demonstrating a fixed superior ability, whereas performance-avoidance goals focus on hiding a fixed inferior ability.

Research shows a meaningful pattern in how these goals relate to mindset. According to a meta-analysis study based on survey studies, a growth mindset was positively related with mastery goals, which was consistent with earlier experimental studies. As expected, both performance-approach and performance-avoidance goals had a negative relationship with a growth mindset, with this negative relationship stronger for performance-avoidance goals.

## The Role of Failure as an Ego-Threatening Event

Importantly, the connection between mindset and goals intensifies precisely when failure occurs. The same meta-analysis study found that the relationship between a growth mindset and achievement goals becomes stronger in ego-threatening situations, which are defined as any events or situations that have an unfavorable effect on the self. Considering that a failure experience is a common ego-threatening event in academic settings, a stronger relationship between a growth mindset and achievement goals can be found following failure.

This effect appears strongest among those who have actually experienced setbacks. Compared to students who received higher scores, those who received lower scores had a stronger relationship between a growth mindset and mastery goals.

## Why Fixed Mindsets Lead to Avoidance

The underlying psychology explains the avoidance behavior. People with a fixed mindset tend to see intelligence or talent as a limited quantity. Challenge can feel threatening because struggle suggests low ability. As a result, people may avoid hard tasks, hide mistakes, discount feedback, or give up when success is not immediate.

This can compound over time into what Dweck termed "low-effort syndrome." Students with an academic fixed mindset eventually developed "low-effort syndrome" (Dweck, 2006, p. 58). To protect their egos, students with low-effort syndrome stopped attempting challenging tasks because by avoiding the task, they avoided failure. As a result, low-effort syndrome lowered students' motivation to learn and led to a decline in their overall academic achievement.

The threat to self-image is central to this dynamic. Students with a fixed-intelligence mindset may feel threatened at the notion of their flaws being unmasked because they believe their flaws result in failures. Therefore, they might be unwilling to attempt challenging tasks.

---

**Summary of the chain:** A fixed mindset (belief that ability is immutable) → tendency to adopt performance goals, especially performance-avoidance goals aimed at hiding perceived inferior ability → a helpless response to failure characterized by withdrawal and disengagement. Conversely, a growth mindset → mastery goals → a resilient, learning-oriented response to setbacks. Notably, this relationship between mindset and goal adoption becomes most pronounced precisely in the wake of failure, since failure functions as an ego-threatening event.

A useful caveat from the research is that mindsets occur in a continuum between the fixed and growth extremes and are domain specific.

Here's what the research reveals about how attachment styles influence academic help-seeking behavior:

## Attachment Theory Foundations

Attachment styles develop from early caregiving experiences and shape how people seek support throughout life. The purpose of the attachment system is to provide safety by regulating proximity-seeking behavior, which allows for the attainment of care and support from an attachment figure. People whose needs for proximity are satisfied experience attachment securely and tend to expect these responses from other relationship partners. However, when needs for proximity are discouraged or go unmet, people experience attachment insecurity, and the insecure attachment style (anxious or avoidant attachment) is formed to attempt other coping strategies.

A useful distinction between the two insecure styles: Anxious attachment assesses individuals' beliefs about self-worth and whether they will be included by others, while avoidant attachment assesses individuals' beliefs about others and whether they feel comfortable approaching them.

## Avoidant Attachment and Help-Seeking

Avoidant attachment is most strongly linked to the *reluctance to seek help*. Avoidant attachment may lead to emotional detachment, reluctance to seek help, and challenges with sustained motivation. This carries real academic costs: avoiding attachment aversion to seeking help can lead to a decline in the received support and academic commitment, in which case the learners can fail in class.

A key psychological mechanism is that avoidant learners equate asking for help with weakness. They could fumble over the job on their own instead of seeking assistance where they can get it, since asking for help is synonymous with being incompetent. More broadly, insecure attachment is also associated with pessimistic beliefs and expectations about the risks, costs, and futility of seeking help from others, and with subjective perceptions of available support.

## Anxious Attachment and Help-Seeking

Anxious attachment presents a more complex picture. On one hand, those with a preoccupied or anxious attachment style often crave closeness and reassurance, leading them to seek support frequently. However, their heightened emotional reactivity and fear of rejection may make their support-seeking less effective. Interestingly, one study found a counterintuitive pattern: participants with a dismissing attachment style had the highest mean score on seeking social support, while those with an anxious-preoccupied style had the lowest mean score. However, these differences were not statistically significant.

In terms of academic outcomes, anxious attachment may manifest as irregular class attendance, low self-esteem, diminished motivation, and inconsistent performance. More generally, an anxious state is associated with academic maladjustment, such as a decrease in self-esteem, enhanced anxiety, stress, burnout, and problems with time management and delay.

## Academic Help-Seeking as a Learning Strategy

Help-seeking is widely understood as an adaptive self-regulation skill rather than a sign of dependence. To seek help in such circumstances, students should be able to monitor their understanding, recognize their needs for seeking help, and translate this recognition into action. In other words, academic help-seeking consists of students' cognition, motivation, and behavior regulation. Accordingly, it has been consistently conceived of as a self-regulated learning strategy, which enables students to perform a more active and constructive role in their learning.

The benefits are well documented: college students' adaptive help-seeking, asking for hints or explanations necessary for learning and task mastery, has been linked to greater cognitive and behavioral engagement, less anxiety, and better academic performance.

Researchers distinguish several types of help-seeking behavior. Academic help seeking includes instrumental help seeking from teacher, instrumental help seeking from classmate, executive help seeking (students attempt to avoid work by asking others for answers to problems), and avoidance of help seeking (students would rather write an answer than ask others for the answer to the problem).

## The Cost of Avoiding Help

The reluctance to seek help has measurable academic consequences. Although college students are generally able to monitor their learning processes and recognize gaps in their skills or knowledge, some students are reluctant to ask for much-needed help from their instructors and peers. Asking for help may be regarded as a sign of personal inadequacy and overdependence, leading to embarrassment and loss of self-esteem. More importantly, it has been claimed that by avoiding help-seeking when needed, students place themselves in a disadvantageous position for academic success.

Empirical evidence supports this across age groups: college students' avoidant help-seeking was related to their lower exam performance and higher anxiety. Similarly, college students' avoidant help-seeking was negatively related to academic performance. These patterns also hold among younger students, as adolescent students' avoidant help-seeking has been negatively associated with test scores and grade point average and positively with anxiety.

---

**Summary:** The research suggests that both insecure attachment styles can undermine effective academic help-seeking, but through different pathways—**avoidant** learners tend to withdraw and self-isolate (viewing help as a sign of incompetence), while **anxious** learners may seek support but in ways complicated by fear of rejection and emotional reactivity. In both cases, the failure to engage in adaptive help-seeking is associated with poorer academic performance and higher anxiety. # Gross's Process Model of Emotion Regulation

James Gross developed an influential process model of emotion regulation that distinguishes between two broad categories of regulation strategies based on *when* they intervene in the emotion-generative process.

## The Core Distinction

The model's central organizing principle separates strategies by their temporal placement. As emotions unfold over time they can be regulated along many points on a temporal sequence ranging from early processes like cue evaluation to later processes like response modulation. Antecedent-focused emotion-regulation strategies modulate nascent emotional responses. In contrast, response-focused emotion-regulation strategies modulate fully formed, ongoing emotional responses. These are the central tenets of Gross' process model of emotion regulation.

## The Five-Stage Framework

The process model maps onto the emotion-generative timeline through a sequence of intervention points. The framework consists of five boxes arranged horizontally in a sequence, labeled from left to right as: "Situation selection," "Situation modification," "Attentional deployment (distraction, concentration)," "Cognitive change (reappraisal)," and "Response modulation (suppression)." Arrows point downward from each box to a horizontal line beneath them, labeled "Situation," "Attention," "Appraisal," and "Response."

Importantly, a box labeled "Antecedent-focused strategies" is positioned below the first four stages, while "Response-focused strategies" is beneath the last stage. This means that most of the emotion regulation points proposed by this process model are antecedent-focused or happen before the emotion response. Only response modulation is response-focused, occurring after the emotional response.

## Reappraisal vs. Suppression

The two most-studied strategies represent each category:

**Cognitive Reappraisal (antecedent-focused):** Cognitive reappraisal is an antecedent-focused strategy that involves interpreting a potential emotion elicitor in a way that heightens or lessens its emotional impact. It is aimed at modifying the emotional meaning and impact of a situation that elicits emotion.

**Expressive Suppression (response-focused):** Expressive suppression is response-focused and a form of response modulation, which involves inhibiting or suppressing an emotional experience once it has been activated or solidified. Because suppression comes later in the emotion-generative process, it does not influence the emotion itself, but rather its outcomes.

## Divergent Consequences

Gross's seminal 1998 study tested this distinction empirically. Using a process model of emotion, a distinction between antecedent-focused and response-focused emotion regulation is proposed. To test this distinction, 120 participants were shown a disgusting film while their experiential, behavioral, and physiological responses were recorded.

The experimental design involved three conditions: participants were told to either (a) think about the film in such a way that they would feel nothing (reappraisal, a form of antecedent-focused emotion regulation), (b) behave in such a way that someone watching them would not know they were feeling anything (suppression, a form of response-focused emotion regulation), or (c) watch the film (a control condition).

The results revealed key differences between the strategies. Compared with the control condition, both reappraisal and suppression were effective in reducing emotion-expressive behavior. However, reappraisal decreased disgust experience, whereas suppression increased sympathetic activation. These results suggest that these 2 emotion regulatory processes may have different adaptive consequences.

## Temporal Dynamics

Research using neural and physiological measures has supported the model's predictions about timing. It was shown that distraction reduced emotional responding prior to cognitive reappraisal, and reappraisal in turn exerted its influence earlier than expressive suppression, confirming predictions derived from the process model of emotion regulation.

This reflects the broader logic of the model, in which emotion generation is a dynamic process that is based upon specific cognitive processes and unfolds over time. After encountering an emotive situation, attentional deployment towards the emotional stimulus is followed by the identification of the situation's meaning. These cognitive processes give rise to the emotional response that involves changes in physiological, cognitive-emotional, and behavioral response systems.

# The Window of Tolerance: Affect Regulation and Arousal States

## Origins of the Concept

The "window of tolerance" is a foundational concept in trauma psychology and affect regulation. The 'window of tolerance' was first introduced by Dan Siegel (1999) as a way to conceptualize the optimal zone of arousal in which an individual can function effectively — emotionally regulated, cognitively flexible, and socially engaged. More specifically, the window of tolerance is a model of autonomic arousal proposed by Siegel (1999) that focuses specifically on understanding the body's nervous system regulation after experiencing trauma.

## The Optimal Zone

Within this window, a person operates at their best. Within this window, individuals are able to process stimuli without becoming overwhelmed or shutting down. From a neurobiological standpoint, this is where the prefrontal cortex (the brain's rational, executive-functioning control center) remains fully online. When you are within your Window of Tolerance, you have access to all of your executive functioning skills like organizing, planning, regulating emotions, and problem-solving effectively.

## The Two Extremes of Dysregulation

When arousal moves outside this optimal zone, two distinct patterns of dysregulation can occur:

**Hyperarousal (above the window):** When arousal exceeds the upper threshold, clients may experience hyperarousal (e.g., panic, irritability, impulsivity), while dropping below the lower threshold can lead to hypoarousal (e.g., emotional numbing, dissociation, withdrawal). In this state, the sympathetic nervous system is stuck in the "on" position and a person may find themselves irritable, panicky, hypervigilant, or physically wired while their heart is pounding, their mind is racing, and their body is unable to settle.

**Hypoarousal (below the window):** When you're in hypoarousal, the parasympathetic nervous system hits the brakes hard and you move into a state of shutdown, aka a "freeze response." This comes with emotional numbness, low energy, withdrawal, cognitive fog, and disconnection from one's self and others. Notably, it's possible for someone in hypoarousal to look "fine" on the outside; as they are likely not screaming or crying, but rather quite flat.

## Connection to Trauma and the Autonomic Nervous System

The model is deeply tied to how the autonomic nervous system responds to trauma. A comprehensive review describes how the window of tolerance describes optimal affective functioning within a "window" of moderate arousal, with unpleasant dysregulation occurring when activation shifts toward hyperarousal (fight/flight) or hypoarousal (freeze/collapse). Autonomic arousal in the wake of trauma: sympathetic hyperarousal and parasympathetic hypoarousal states drive emotional and autonomic dysregulation. Importantly, there is also a frozen fear state in which both extremes may be present, and states of optimal arousal and emotional regulation are relatively rare or difficult to maintain.

Trauma directly affects the width of this window. Dr. Dan Siegel developed the window of tolerance to illustrate a person's ability to regulate their emotions and not become overwhelmed. When someone experiences trauma, their brain may become more attuned to detecting threats quickly as a survival mechanism. This heightened state of alertness can persist, reducing their window of tolerance and making them more prone to anticipating threats.

## Integration with Polyvagal Theory

Siegel's model is often paired with Stephen Porges' work. Siegel's work is complemented by Porges' Polyvagal Theory (2011), which describes how shifts in autonomic states — particularly involving the vagus nerve — influence physiological readiness, perception of safety, and social engagement. The states map onto each other directly: Siegel's window of tolerance corresponds directly to the ventral vagal state. When you're within your window, your nervous system reads the environment as safe enough for social engagement, clear thinking, and flexible responses. Moving into hyperarousal reflects sympathetic activation, while hypoarousal corresponds to dorsal vagal shutdown.

## Clinical Relevance

The width of a person's window varies, particularly among those with trauma histories. People who have experienced trauma, chronic stress, or adverse experiences often have a narrower window of tolerance, making them more easily dysregulated. This means they may quickly shift into hyperarousal or hypoarousal in response to stress.

The model has broad clinical applications across diagnoses:
- Clients with PTSD often fluctuate between states of hyperarousal (e.g., hypervigilance, irritability) and hypoarousal (e.g., dissociation, emotional numbing).
- Individuals with C-PTSD frequently experience sustained dysregulation, including chronic emotional overwhelm and shutdown responses.
- People with GAD may spend much of their time near or above the upper threshold of their window, marked by constant worry, restlessness, and physiological tension.

## Returning to the Window

Several approaches can help expand or return a person to their window of tolerance. Mindfulness and grounding techniques (e.g., deep breathing, body awareness, meditation) can help bring a person back into their window. Co-regulation with supportive relationships (e.g., therapists, friends, or loved ones) can assist in emotional regulation. Therapy (e.g., Somatic Experiencing, EMDR, DBT, or CFT) can help individuals process trauma and develop better emotional regulation skills. Physical practices like yoga, exercise, and breathwork can also help regulate the nervous system.

---

**Note on sources:** Much of the foundational material traces to Siegel's 1999 work *The Developing Mind* and Pat Ogden's somatic adaptations (Ogden et al., 2006). If you need the primary academic sources, the ResearchGate review on "Autonomic dysregulation and the Window of Tolerance Model" provides a detailed scholarly treatment of the model's application to complex emotional trauma.

Based on the search results, here's an overview of how self-efficacy, autonomy, competence, and challenge relate within self-determination theory and Bandura's work:

## Self-Determination Theory's Core Needs

Self-determination theory provides the foundational framework here. Among motivational frameworks, self-determination theory (SDT) has emerged as one of the most influential and well-established. One major contribution of SDT is that it conceptualizes the three basic psychological needs of autonomy, competence and relatedness as essential and innate for one's psychological growth, internalization and well-being.

The needs are defined as follows: Autonomy reflects one's need to act with a sense of discretion of his/her own behaviors and to feel psychologically self-directed, while relatedness refers to the need to interpersonally connect with others, to give affection, and to receive love and care in return. Finally, competence is defined as the need to feel effective and mastery, and to demonstrate and improve one's abilities.

## The Link Between Competence and Bandura's Self-Efficacy

A key conceptual bridge exists between SDT's competence need and Bandura's self-efficacy concept. Competence is defined as feeling effective when manipulating one's environment (White, 1959), akin to the effort-performance expectancy proposed in expectancy theory (Vroom, 1964) and the self-efficacy concept proposed in social learning theory (Bandura, 1982). This connection has evolutionary significance, since it has evolutionary advantage for survival because it supports learning and adaptation to new environmental conditions.

## Self-Efficacy and the Role of Challenge

Bandura's self-efficacy theory directly addresses how individuals respond to challenges, which is central to your query about challenge as a moderator. Self-efficacy is a person's particular set of beliefs that determine how well one can execute a plan of action in prospective situations (Bandura, 1977). To put it in more simple terms, self-efficacy is a person's belief in their ability to succeed in a particular situation.

The way people perceive and approach challenging tasks depends heavily on their self-efficacy beliefs. Those with low self-efficacy may dwell on deficiencies and magnify potential difficulties, leading to stress and impaired performance. Conversely, individuals with high self-efficacy focus their attention and effort on the task demands, seeing obstacles as challenges that spur greater effort. Additionally, self-efficacy plays a role in self-regulation, determining how much effort is expended, how long someone perseveres in the face of difficulties, and their resilience to setbacks.

This difference in challenge-response is also captured in practical terms: someone with high self-efficacy approaches challenges as problems to be solved. Someone with low self-efficacy may avoid the same challenge altogether, not because they lack ability, but because they doubt their capacity to use it effectively.

## Integrating the Theories

Research has attempted to formally test and integrate these two theoretical frameworks. One model proposes a developmental sequence among the needs: the rationale for this relationship is that autonomy and relatedness should be developed first to then influence competence/self-efficacy. The proposed relationship between the needs of autonomy and relatedness with competence/self-efficacy has some theoretical support.

The autonomy dimension is shaped substantially by environmental conditions, which relates to how challenge functions as a contextual moderator: environments that offer genuine choice, self-direction, and non-controlling feedback cultivate autonomy and, with it, intrinsic motivation. By contrast, environments that impose strict deadlines, threats, surveillance, or excessive rewards undermine it. The overjustification effect illustrates this well: introducing tangible rewards for activities people already enjoy can erode the very motivation those rewards were meant to sustain.

There is also a broader theoretical convergence worth noting: Bandura's self-efficacy, Martin Seligman's learned helplessness, Deci and Ryan's self-determination all agree that confidence plays a significant role in motivation. Core self-evaluations theory suggests that competence (self-efficacy) is a first order core belief from which other self-evaluations build upon.

---

**A note on your query:** The search results strongly support the conceptual links between self-efficacy (Bandura), and SDT's needs of autonomy and competence, as well as the role of challenge in self-efficacy theory. However, I did not find results specifically testing **"challenge" as a statistical moderator** of the self-efficacy/autonomy/competence relationships. If that specific empirical relationship is what you're after, I'd be happy to run a more targeted search.

Here's what I found regarding linguistic markers of anxiety and personality in text, including LIWC-based approaches to detecting individual differences in language.

## Overview of LIWC and Text Analysis

LIWC (Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count) is a foundational tool in this field. The LIWC application is a text analysis software that calculates the degree of use of different word categories in various texts. Empirical results using LIWC demonstrate its ability to detect meaning in a wide variety of experimental settings, including to show attentional focus, emotionality, social relationships, thinking styles, and individual differences.

The theoretical basis for using language to detect individual differences is well-established. The sedimentation hypothesis assumes that descriptors of relevant personality traits are manifested and communicated through language. Since the introduction of automated quantitative text analysis, which allows one to analyze individual differences in language use, there is increasing interest and knowledge about the role of language use in psychology. This approach offers distinct advantages, as it allows one to understand individual differences from a perspective beyond standard self-report questionnaires, showing how traits are expressed and perceived through language.

## Linguistic Markers of Anxiety

Several studies have identified specific linguistic features tied to anxiety:

- A study on Generalized Anxiety Disorder found that significant positive correlations were found between GAD and the following LIWC categories: negations, sadness, personal pronouns, present focus, social processes, family, negative emotions, and anger. Conversely, significant negative correlations were obtained for GAD and longer words, positive emotions, and focus on the future.

- More broadly, researchers have theorized that mental illness reshapes language use. It has been hypothesised by many researchers that mental illness significantly alters one's linguistic style whereby the words used by individuals may indicate the reduced positive emotion, ruminative self-preoccupation, low levels of motivation and pleasure, and difficulty foreseeing positive future events that characterise depressive and anxious states.

- Regarding negative emotional language specifically, negative emotional word frequency is a robust marker in both Chinese and Western settings.

## Linguistic Markers of Personality

Research links language patterns to the Big Five personality dimensions, particularly neuroticism, which is closely tied to anxiety. High neurotics also tend to convey more negative emotions, more anxiety, and negative affiliation to intimate relationships and groups in written texts.

However, these associations tend to be modest. Studies that apply LIWC and its variants to extract word categories that reflect topical content have identified several small to moderate correlations (absolute value typically smaller than 0.4) between LIWC language features and self-reported Big Five personality dimensions.

## Predictive Modeling and Clinical Applications

LIWC features are increasingly used in machine learning pipelines for detection. LIWC is widely used for automatic detection and risk stratification of conditions such as PTSD, depression, anxiety, and suicide probability. In one example, LIWC features achieved 89% accuracy in PTSD detection and outperformed standard lexicon or black-box ML baselines.

For anxiety specifically, combining linguistic and personality features can improve performance. One study reported that increased GAD recognition performance was obtained when facial behavior features were augmented with (Big Five) personality features.

## Important Caveats and Limitations

Notably, the evidence is not uniformly strong, and some recent work raises caution:

- A key limitation of LIWC itself is that there is a notable absence of specific linguistic markers for anxiety in any of the Linguistic Dimensions of the LIWC (pronouns used, prepositions, auxiliary verbs) and also in the sub-domain of specific emotional states.

- A rigorous randomized crossover trial produced notably weak results. Using a randomised cross over trial design, 218 adults provided eight different types of text data of varying frequencies and emotional valance. Linguistic features were extracted using LIWC-22 and correlated with self-reported symptoms. Machine learning was used to determine associations. The conclusion was sobering: no linguistic features were consistently associated with depressive or anxiety symptoms within or across all tasks. Features associated with depressive symptoms were different for each task and there was only some degree of reliability of these features within tasks. In all machine learning models, predicted values were weakly associated with actual values.

- Researchers emphasize methodological rigor, noting they must consider lexicon and context limitations, domain specificity, sample size for stable inference, and the necessity of rigorous psychometric validation when deploying LIWC in novel or cross-domain contexts.

## Future Directions

The field is evolving toward more sophisticated approaches. Ongoing extensions—including domain-adapted lexicons, hybrid deep learning pipelines, and explainability-focused integrations—are extending the utility of LIWC, consolidating its role as a reference standard for computational psycholinguistic analysis.

If you'd like, I can dig deeper into any specific aspect—such as the depression-anxiety distinction, cross-linguistic LIWC adaptations, or the integration of LIWC with deep learning and large language models.

Here's what the research says about calibrating "desirable difficulties" and finding the optimal challenge point—including the risk of making learning too hard.

## The Optimal Challenge Point (OCP)

The core idea is captured in the **challenge point framework**, which is a model based on the relationship between task difficulty and the ability or the knowledge and skills of the learner. This framework identifies the so-called optimal challenge point (OCP), where the learner obtains the greatest potential for learning.

At this sweet spot, learners operate just beyond their current level of mastery. Success is possible, but effortful. Errors are frequent enough to trigger adaptation, but not so frequent that they become discouraging.

## The "Goldilocks" Risk: Too Hard Demotivates

A consistent theme across sources is that difficulty cuts both ways. As one learning podcast framed it through a game analogy, if a game is too hard, people walk away. If it's too easy, people may also walk away. So it's about that right balance. The same goes with learning. If it's too hard, if there's not enough scaffolding, then a difficulty can demotivate a learner. If it's too easy, then that can also demotivate a learner.

From a cognitive standpoint, when the challenge level is low, we may encounter apathy or boredom. Make it too high, though, and anxiety sets in as we worry about making mistakes or failing to achieve the preferred outcome. For a desirable level of difficulty, the task must be achievable. The ideal zone is that sweet spot between your current skill level and the challenge level, where the task cannot be done on autopilot but is feasible to complete—often associated with a flow state.

A key limitation worth flagging: if difficulty is too high, it can lead to frustration, overwhelm, and demotivation, particularly for beginners or learners with low confidence.

## Calibration: The ~85% Rule

Research offers a surprisingly concrete benchmark for calibration. When scientists analyzed how fast learning happens under specific conditions, they discovered something striking: the golden zone is where you're right about 85 percent of the time and wrong 15 percent. In that range, they observed that learning accelerated.

In classroom retrieval-practice contexts, a similar (slightly looser) target is recommended: researchers recommend that students should be getting a success rate of around 80% when trying to retrieve prior learning. So, you might aim to pitch the quiz at a difficulty level that means most learners are getting a few answers wrong.

Importantly, this is a guiding principle rather than a rigid formula. The idea of the optimal challenge is a qualitative framework backed by empirical data, but unlike other theories in cognitive science (such as cognitive load theory), it's hard to quantify universally. Think of it as a guiding principle, not a precise formula.

## Factors That Shift Where "Just Hard Enough" Falls

Calibration must be personalized, because the right level varies by learner and context:

- **Individual differences:** The level of difficulty involved might be expected to vary among learners. What one learner finds quite difficult may be impossibly challenging for another, perhaps leading them to give up entirely.

- **Motivation, scaffolding, and fatigue:** A motivated learner can handle more complexity. A well-scaffolded task (one that starts easy and becomes more difficult step by step) lowers the difficulty without dumbing things down. Even your level of focus or fatigue shifts where the "just hard enough" line falls.

## When a Difficulty Stops Being "Desirable"

The critical caveat is that difficulty must be matched to prerequisite knowledge. According to a 2018 study cited by KQED, "If a learner does not have the background knowledge or skills to respond successfully to a given difficulty, it becomes an undesirable difficulty."

The recommended fix is to adjust the level rather than remove the challenge entirely: these strategies shouldn't be seen as dispensable, able to be dropped if students are finding things too challenging. What can be changed is the level of challenge, and this is surprisingly straightforward. However, it is best tackled one strategy at a time. For struggling learners specifically, the way to adjust is not to dispose of the task entirely, but to modify the difficulty level for different students, while ensuring that all are still prompted to retrieve.

## The Motivation Connection

Finally, perceived value matters as much as raw difficulty. If a task is too complex or makes no sense to the student, they may be hard pushed to find value in the activity which can lead to disengagement and demotivation. Motivation plays a crucial role in learning and is heavily influenced by the value students place on a task. Conversely, when students find value in the difficulty, motivation to engage with the task increases.

---

**Bottom line:** The goal is to pitch tasks just beyond current mastery—targeting roughly an 80–85% success rate—while ensuring learners have the prerequisite knowledge and adequate scaffolding. Push too far past that point and the difficulty stops being "desirable," tipping learners from productive struggle into frustration, anxiety, and disengagement.

Here's what I found on measuring implicit theories of intelligence and detecting fixed vs. growth mindsets, including approaches that go beyond traditional self-report and toward language/behavioral cues:

## The Standard Measure: Implicit Theories of Intelligence Scale (ITIS)

The most widely used tool is a self-report questionnaire. Mindset beliefs are typically measured using the Implicit Theories of Intelligence Scale, which consists of eight items: four growth and four fixed (Dweck, 1999; Cook et al., 2017; Sisk et al., 2018).

An important methodological caveat concerns how these items relate to one another. A large item-level meta-analysis examined a long-standing assumption in the field. Fixed and growth mindsets represent implicit theories about the nature of one's abilities or traits. The existing body of research on academic achievement and the effectiveness of mindset interventions for student learning largely relies on the premise that fixed and growth mindsets are mutually exclusive. This premise has led to the common practice in which measures of one mindset are reversed and then assumed to represent the other mindset.

That study challenged this practice. Focusing on K-12 and university students (N = 27328), they tested the validity of this practice via a comprehensive item-level meta-analysis of the Implicit Theories of Intelligence Scale (ITIS). The findings were significant: they found positive item-item correlations within the sets of fixed and growth mindset items, with substantial between-study heterogeneity. The ITIS factor structure comprised two moderately correlated mindset factors (= 0.63–0.65), even after reversing one mindset scale. Ultimately, they argue that fixed and growth mindsets are not mutually exclusive but correlated constructs.

## Beyond Self-Report: Implicit (Behavioral) Measurement

The query's interest in detecting mindsets through cues rather than self-report connects directly to a notable critique and innovation. Researchers have pointed out a conceptual mismatch: although the theory presumes implicit processes (i.e., unaware beliefs, guiding behaviors and actions automatically), the concept is typically assessed with self-reports.

To address this, one research team developed a non-self-report measure. They brought together research on intelligence mindset with research on implicit social cognition. Harnessing recent innovations from research on implicit measures, they assessed intelligence mindsets on an implicit level with a mousetracking Propositional Evaluation Paradigm. This measure captures the spontaneous truth evaluation of growth- and fixed-mindset statements to tap into implicit beliefs.

This approach is the closest analog in the literature to "detecting" mindset from real-time cues (here, mouse-movement trajectories while evaluating statements). The results showed it added predictive value: in two preregistered laboratory studies (N = 184; N = 193), they found that implicitly measured growth mindsets predicted learning engagement after an experience of failure above and beyond the explicit measure. The authors note this represents the first exploration into the implicit theories of intelligence mindset beyond self-report.

A key implication is that implicit and explicit aspects of intelligence mindsets must be differentiated. People might be in a different mindset when making learning-related decisions under optimal conditions (i.e., with ample time and capacity) versus under pressure.

## Why Mindset Cues Matter (Behavioral Signatures)

The reason mindset is detectable through behavior relates to how it functions. Decades of research demonstrates how mindsets act as meaning systems that influence how students interpret and respond to academic cues, especially negative feedback and failure (Hong et al., 1999). Specifically, students who believe that their intelligence is fixed tend to avoid challenging situations where they might receive negative feedback, which is threatening because it is seen as a permanent and personal indictment of their fixed abilities. As a result, receiving negative feedback (such as failing an exam) is discouraging, and they are more likely to withdraw and disengage.

Based on the search results, here is an overview of the research on attachment security priming and the broaden-and-build cycle, particularly the work by Mikulincer and Shaver:

## The Broaden-and-Build Cycle of Attachment Security

The core concept comes from Mikulincer and Shaver, who built on Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory of positive emotions. Experimental studies have shown that correlational findings reflect the action of what they call a broaden-and-build cycle of attachment security. This cycle is a cascade of mental and behavioral events that flows from the activation of mental representations of attachment security to greater emotional equanimity, better personal and social adjustment, more satisfying close relationships, and autonomous personal growth.

## The Secure Base and the Dual Function Model

A key distinction in this research concerns *when* security priming activates exploration versus threat-reduction. In a context in which there is no immediate threat (e.g., the stress level is low or there is no obvious threat), security priming is likely to activate the sense of secure base, and to contribute to what Mikulincer and Shaver refer to as the 'broaden and build cycle' of attachment security. They suggest that security increases people's resilience and expands their skills and capabilities as well as their problem-solving abilities and cognitive flexibility.

The secure base script involves a particular set of beliefs: this script entails declarative and procedural knowledge that the world is safe and that one can call upon attachment figures when needed. Knowing these things, one can devote attention and effort to personal growth, self-development, and the needs of others. This script is a good depiction of the secure base aspect of security.

## Empirical Evidence for Broadening Effects

Several studies demonstrate that security priming promotes exploration and challenge engagement:

- **Exploration and novelty:** Green and Campbell asked people to read generic sentences describing secure or insecure close relationships and found that a secure prime, compared with an insecure prime, led to greater endorsement of exploration-related behavior and greater liking for novel pictures.

- **Vitality and learning:** Luke, Sedikides, and Carnelley found that security priming, as compared with neutral priming, increased both vitality and willingness to learn and that these effects could not be explained by positive affect.

- **Creative problem-solving:** Mikulincer, Shaver, and Rom found that implicit exposure to the name of a security provider (nominated in the WHOTO) led to better performance on a creative problem-solving task than implicit exposure to the names of others who were not nominated as attachment figures.

## Extension to Prosocial Behavior

The broadening effects extend beyond personal exploration to caring for others. The broadening effects of a laboratory security enhancement are also evident in prosocial feelings and behaviors. Specifically, both implicit and explicit forms of security priming increased feelings of compassion and actual helping behavior toward a stranger who was becoming increasingly distressed while performing a series of aversive tasks.

## Recent Applications to Exploration and Challenge

More recent work directly connects security priming to engaging with life challenges. Participants primed with a secure relationship utilised their close others' mental presence as a secure base, increasing their exploratory behaviour motivations in intellectual, social and environmental areas in line with the broaden-and-build cycle of secure relationships. The researchers concluded that by using guided imagery techniques, people's motivations towards challenges in life can be increased (e.g., financial investments).

## Important Caveats

The benefits of security priming are not universal. Caution is urged regarding the conclusion that secure attachment primes have beneficial effects for nearly everyone. New experimental evidence suggests attachment anxiety may be associated with undesirable changes in affect following some secure attachment primes. Additionally, priming security may affect individuals differently as a function of their chronic accessibility of secure working models, which is defined by their attachment orientation—a model that fully accounts for this possibility takes into account participants' dispositional attachment orientation (levels of avoidance and anxiety).

**Key sources** include Mikulincer & Shaver's 2020 article "Broaden-and-Build Effects of Contextually Boosting the Sense of Attachment Security in Adulthood" (published in *Current Directions in Psychological Science* via SAGE) and the more comprehensive open-access review "Enhancing the 'Broaden and Build' Cycle of Attachment Security in Adulthood" available through PMC, which would be excellent starting points if you'd like to read the primary literature directly.

# Summary: NFC and PSE in Responses to Failure

## Core Findings

**Study setup:** 194 participants completed solvable and unsolvable anagram/tangram tasks; researchers measured state anger after each task and intention to persist after failures.

## Emotional Response (Anger)

- NFC positively predicted anger specifically **after failure**, not at baseline or after success. There was a "positive effect of NFC on anger after failure" (b = 2.04, p < .001).
- Higher-NFC individuals showed stronger anger after failing cognitively demanding tasks—consistent with their motivation to avoid failure and an "incompetent self-image."

## The NFC × PSE Interaction

This is the central mechanism. PSE **moderated** NFC's effect on anger:
- When PSE was **low**, NFC had no relationship with anger (b = 0.03, p = .801).
- When PSE was **moderate or high**, NFC predicted anger (b = 0.22 and b = 0.42 respectively, both p < .001).
- Directional claim: "the higher an individual's PSE was, the more did their NFC affect their anger after failure."

**Mechanism:** Individuals who believe in their competence (PSE) *and* invest effort (NFC) don't expect failure, so failing produces greater anger/frustration. As the authors summarize, only with "medium to high PSE" will cognitive motivation positively affect anger.

## Behavioral Response (Persistence)

- NFC and PSE both **directly and positively** predicted intention to persist.
- Anger alone had **no direct effect** on persistence.
- A significant **three-way interaction** (NFC × PSE × anger) emerged: persistence probability was "highest when NFC is high and also PSE as well as anger are greater than the mean."

## Who Persists vs. Disengages

- **Persist:** High NFC + high PSE + high anger → anger becomes an activating impulse driving persistence. NFC also boosted persistence even when anger/PSE were low.
- **Disengage:** Low PSE individuals showed high anger regardless of NFC but "a very low probability to intent to persist." Their anger likely reflects perceived lack of ability, prompting escape rather than continued effort.

## Key Mechanism Claims

1. Anger functions as an "activating affect" tied to approach motivation—but only when paired with high NFC and PSE (control/competence beliefs).
2. Low-PSE individuals may feel "confirmed in their expectation of not being able to solve a task," producing anger without persistence.
3. High-PSE/NFC individuals integrate experiences into self-concept and feel more confident, amplifying frustration when failing.

**Limitations noted:** Single-item persistence measure (intention, not actual behavior); biased non-representative sample; STAXI may underweight low-level anger.

# The Dual Function Model of Security Priming (DFSP)

## Core Framework

The model proposes that activating attachment security cues triggers one of two functions, mirroring how a security-providing attachment figure operates:

- **Safe haven (stress relief)**: provision of comfort and reassurance to reduce stress
- **Secure base (mobilization)**: facilitation of exploration and promotion of autonomy

The key determinant is **the level of stress imposed by the context** and how the individual appraises it (threat vs. challenge).

## When Each Function Activates

**Threat-reduction (safe haven) — high-stress contexts:** When someone faces a threat, priming activates an "if-then" script: seek protection, expect responsiveness, regain security. The authors note people "may avoid action and focus inwardly on the self and on stress reduction."

**Broaden-and-build (secure base) — low/no-threat contexts:** With no immediate threat, priming signals "the world is safe," freeing the person to explore, self-develop, and attend to others. This contributes to expanded resilience, skills, and cognitive flexibility.

## Empirical Evidence (Cortisol Study)

The study tested HPA-axis activity using salivary cortisol:
- **Priming *after* a stressor → cortisol decreased** (stress relief)
- **Priming *before* a stressor → cortisol increased** (energy mobilization for action)

Cortisol works as a marker because it is released "not only in response to stress, but also more generally when energy needs to be mobilized."

## Effect of Chronic Attachment Orientation

**Attachment anxiety** (mobilization condition): Higher anxiety was linked to higher peak cortisol and **slower recovery to baseline**. Proposed explanation: priming security may simultaneously activate "a sense of security and anxiety of being abandoned," since anxious individuals show "strong relational ambivalence." Rumination on negative memories may also slow recovery.

**Fearful avoidants** (high anxiety + high avoidance): showed **higher baseline cortisol**.

**Stress-relief effect was robust:** post-stressor priming reduced cortisol "regardless of attachment scores."

## Concrete Claims for Calibrating Support vs. Challenge

1. **Match intervention to stress level**: Use comforting/safe-haven support when someone is under acute stress; use encouragement toward exploration/action when stress is low.
2. **Security priming is context-dependent**, helping explain inconsistent ("replicability") priming findings — context is an input that shapes the effect.
3. **Anxious individuals may need more recovery time** and may experience priming as partly stressful; the safe-haven pathway may be especially relevant for them (the authors pose this as an open question).
4. **Resource appraisal matters**: in high stress, people perceive demands exceeding resources and turn inward; in low stress, they have resources to engage outward (exploring, helping others).

## Caveats

The authors stress this is **preliminary** evidence with notable limitations: no control group, no psychological (subjective) measures of stress/mobilization, no measure of breakup severity, and a possible confound that cortisol increases reflected excitement/arousal rather than mobilization. They call for future replication with varied primes and measures.

Here's what the research and clinical literature say about "rolling with resistance," evoking change talk vs. sustain talk, and the role of psychological reactance in Motivational Interviewing (MI).

## What "Rolling with Resistance" Means

Rolling with resistance is a core MI strategy in which the counselor avoids arguing with or confronting the client. Confronting clients can evoke reactance and shut them down. Therefore, MI counselors "roll with resistance" rather than attempt to argue with the client.

Practically, this involves the counselor essentially aligning with the client's perspective rather than pushing against it. The counselor "pulls up alongside clients," essentially agreeing with the client, even if the statement is factually incorrect or unfairly places blame on others. The therapeutic value of this is that such reflections help capture the client's reasons for not changing and allow them to express their resistance without feeling pressured to change or worrying about being judged.

The technique also reframes resistance itself as a signal rather than an obstacle. Resistance that a person offers can be turned or reframed slightly to create a new momentum toward change—client "resistance" is a signal for the counselor to shift approach.

## The Connection to Reactance

Psychological reactance is central to why MI avoids confrontation. By rolling with resistance, you also avoid reinforcing the client's resistance or triggering their reactance, which is the tendency to do the opposite of what someone tells them to do.

The benefits extend beyond simply avoiding reactance. Rolling with resistance is effective because it helps the client feel heard and respected, which can increase their trust and rapport with you. It also helps the client express their own reasons for change, rather than hearing them from you. This can enhance their intrinsic motivation and self-efficacy, which are key factors for successful behavior change.

You would deploy this technique reactively—you can roll with resistance whenever you notice that the client is showing signs of resistance, such as arguing, denying, ignoring, or minimizing the problem.

## Change Talk vs. Sustain Talk: The Markers

Modern MI distinguishes between two categories of "resistance talk." MI identifies two types of 'resistance talk': (i) sustain talk and (ii) discord or interpersonal resistance.

**Sustain talk** is the client's own language favoring the status quo. 'Sustain talk' involves statements about sustaining a behaviour and not changing, including direct intentions not to change (e.g. 'You can tell me all you want, I'm not going to stop drinking with my mates'), the advantages of the status quo (e.g. 'Drinking is the only way to really relax'), and pessimism about ability to change.

**Change talk**, by contrast, is the client's own language favoring movement toward change. Change talk refers to the client's own arguments for change. It refers to any client comments that reflect movement toward change. The key markers or categories of change talk include disadvantages of the status quo, advantages of change, optimism for change, and intention to change.

## Evoking Change Talk

Evoking is one of MI's four core processes (engaging, focusing, evoking, planning). Evoking is eliciting the person's own perspective, the person's own motivation, and the person's own arguments for change.

The mechanism behind why this works rests on self-persuasion: elicit and reinforce your client's argument for change. As a person argues for one position (positive or negative), he becomes more committed to it. "As I hear myself talk, I learn what I believe."

Specific techniques for evoking change talk include evocative questions, asking for elaboration, querying extremes, looking back, looking forward, and exploring values and goals.

## Why the Balance Matters (Outcomes)

The ratio of change talk to sustain talk has measurable behavioral significance. MI elicits personal statements for change, called change talk, and deals with reasons against change, i.e., sustain talk, within an atmosphere of acceptance and compassion. Research on the associations between MI and behavioral outcomes showed that a higher proportion of change talk over sustain talk is associated with reduced risk-seeking behavior.

Notably, rolling with resistance can actually *reduce* sustain talk—particularly with clients who aren't yet ready to change. Motivational Interviewing with individuals in the pre-contemplation stage represents a use case in which MI processes excel beyond other methods. If the individual is in this stage, they may not be consciously aware of, accepting of, or consider they have a problem. Motivational interviewers in this situation are trained to use processes like rolling with resistance, which reduces a client's need to repeat and reframe their own sustain talk.

---

**A terminology note:** It's worth knowing that in the most recent editions of Miller and Rollnick's foundational MI text, the term "resistance" has largely been replaced and split into "sustain talk" and "discord," reflecting the view that what was once called resistance is often a normal, expected product of the interaction rather than a fixed client trait. Some sources also frame it as a problem with the interviewer's approach, rather than a problem with the client. If you'd like, I can search for more detail on this updated framework (sustain talk vs. discord) or on the empirical evidence linking change talk to clinical outcomes.

# Change Talk, Sustain Talk, and the MISC Coding System

Here's a comprehensive overview of how motivational interviewing (MI) language is categorized and how it relates to clinical outcomes.

## Core Definitions

In MI, client language is categorized along two opposing dimensions. "Change talk" (CT) has been defined as client expressions of the benefits of change, hope or optimism around change, or dissatisfaction with current behavior, while "sustain talk" (ST) is defined as client expressions of the benefits of the status quo, pessimism around change, or satisfaction with current behavior.

A key conceptual development was framing these as two sides of one construct. Change talk is a generic term that encompasses all types of language in favor of change, while sustain talk is a generic term for language that moves away from change or towards the status quo—separating sustain talk from other responses labeled as resistance and counter-change talk.

## The DARN-CAT Framework

The acronym used to delineate types of change talk is DARN-CAT. The acronym DARN CAT helps identify types of change talk: Desire, Ability, Reason, Need, Commitment, Activation, and Taking Steps.

This breaks down into two stages of change talk:

- **Preparatory change talk (DARN):** Preparatory change talk does not necessarily lead to change, but often precedes stronger change talk. It includes Desire ("I want to"), Ability ("I could"), Reasons ("...because"), and Need ("I have to").

- **Mobilizing change talk (CAT):** Mobilizing change talk takes it one step further and there is research evidence that if it is spontaneous, it is most predictive of positive outcomes in MI. It includes Commitment ("I will"), Activation, and Taking Steps.

## The MISC Coding System

The Motivational Interviewing Skill Code (MISC) is the instrument used to code these utterances. Developed to evaluate training, the MISC also became very useful in process research.

In practice, coders apply these categories to both directions of speech. Patient utterances were coded for change talk (CT) or sustain talk (ST) in one of seven categories: Desire, Ability, Reasons, Need, Commitment, Taking Steps, and Other. For each of the client behavior count categories, a further distinction was made as to whether the client's statement was for or against change. When the client made a statement in favor of change, it was coded as Change Talk (CT), and when the statement was against change (or in favor of the status quo), it was coded as Sustain Talk (ST).

Utterances without clear directionality receive a neutral code. Utterances received a neutral code if they did not focus on a target behavior or did not have clear motivational significance as either supporting change or sustaining behavior.

## Origins of Commitment Language Research (Amrhein, 2003)

The seminal study connecting language to outcomes came from Amrhein and colleagues. In an important initial study, Amrhein et al. Notably, the first studies examining the language of change with outcomes failed to find a correlation, making Amrhein's contribution especially significant.

An important contribution of Amrhein's study was empirical support for subtypes of change and sustain talk, specifically desire, ability, reasons, need, and commitment to change.

## Relationship to Clinical Outcomes

The evidence consistently links these language categories to treatment results:

- **Sustain talk predicts worse outcomes:** Greater frequency of client sustain talk in sessions is linked to poorer substance use treatment outcomes.

- **Change talk and commitment language predict better outcomes:** Conversely, MI-consistent counselor behavior focused on eliciting and reflecting change talk, more client change talk compared with sustain talk, and stronger commitment change talk are linked to better substance use outcomes.

- **Counselor behavior matters:** The therapist's role is central, as counselor empathy is also linked to eliciting client change talk. This is why in MI, your main goal is to evoke change talk and minimize evoking or reinforcing sustain talk in counseling sessions.

# Rupture and Repair in the Therapeutic Alliance: The Safran & Muran Process Model

## Foundational Concept

The rupture-repair model is one of the most influential frameworks in psychotherapy research. The rupture-repair model represents one of the most important innovations in therapeutic alliance research and practice since the early 1990s. This model provides a comprehensive and dynamic representation of the therapeutic alliance, especially of its complex management in the therapeutic process.

Building on Bordin's reformulation of the alliance, the model revolves around the construct of rupture, which was defined as "strains in the alliance…consisting either of disagreements about the tasks or goals of therapy or of problems in the bond dimension." Importantly, the term is used broadly: while in common language the word rupture may imply a major conflict or breakdown, in the alliance literature the term is used to refer to a broad range of alliance strains, from minor tensions to major rifts.

## The Two Types of Rupture Markers

Safran and Muran identified two principal categories of rupture. Safran and Muran present two empirically derived stage-process models to conceptualize and facilitate the resolution of therapeutic alliance ruptures, distinguishing between withdrawal ruptures (marked by disengagement or avoidance) and confrontation ruptures (marked by direct aggression or criticism).

### Withdrawal Markers
Withdrawal markers include movements away from another: movements toward isolation, like going silent or pivoting away with another topic or abstract talk. Withdrawals can also include movements away from some aspect of oneself in an effort to appease the other. More specifically, in withdrawal ruptures, patients tend to deal with difficulties or misunderstandings in the therapeutic relationship by falling silent, offering minimal responses to questions, suddenly shifting topic to an unrelated matter, or becoming overly compliant to the therapist's recommendations.

The deeper function of withdrawal is relational preservation. Withdrawals are understood as efforts to preserve relatedness, to not risk severing ties with another, at the expense of self-definition (or sense of agency).

### Confrontation Markers
As for confrontation markers, these are defined as movements against the other: movements involving aggression or control, like criticisms or manipulations. This can include behaviors such as complaining, criticizing, pushing back, or attempting to exert control. In practice, in a confrontation rupture, the patient may directly express anger, resentment, or dissatisfaction with the therapist or some aspect of the treatment, often in a blaming or demanding fashion.

It is also worth noting that ruptures can encompass elements of both withdrawal and confrontation.

## The Underlying Dialectic

The distinction between the two marker types reflects a deeper tension. The distinction between withdrawal and confrontation markers can be understood as reflecting different ways of coping with the dialectical tension between two fundamental human motivations: the need for agency and the need for relatedness/connection. This is echoed in clinical guidance noting that withdrawal ruptures may indicate a patient's desire for connection, even at the expense of agency, while in confrontation ruptures, patients prioritize their need for agency over their need for connection.

## The Resolution (Repair) Process Models

The process by which ruptures are addressed is the heart of the model. The process by which alliance ruptures are repaired is usually referred to as alliance resolutions or repair. Safran and Muran developed distinct resolution pathways for each rupture type:

Safran and Muran proposed two specific resolution models for withdrawal and confrontation ruptures: In the former, the common progression consists of moving through increasingly clearer articulations of discontent to self-assertion, in which the need for agency is realized. The progression in the resolution of confrontation ruptures consists of moving through feelings of anger, to feelings of disappointment and hurt over having been failed by the therapist, to contacting vulnerability and the wish to be nurtured.

For withdrawal ruptures specifically, the resolution process may involve exploration of interpersonal fears and internalized criticisms that inhibit the expression of negative feelings, as well as providing the patient the latitude to begin to communicate their wishes and needs.

Throughout both pathways, progress is rarely linear. Throughout such progressions, there are often shifts, regardless of rupture type, avoidant movements that reflect anxieties resulting from the fear of being too aggressive or too vulnerable associated with the expectation of retaliation or rejection.

## Nature of the Process Models

These stage-process models should be understood as flexible heuristics rather than rigid scripts. Developed through over a decade of task-analytic research combining intensive single-case analyses with aggregate verification, they serve as heuristic prototypes rather than fixed prescriptions, helping therapists recognize probable sequences and select context-sensitive interventions to transform relational strains into opportunities for growth. Furthermore, the sequences are probabilistic, with no stage essential in every case, and resolution often requires repeated cycling over time to build trust and deepen exploration. Both models share core processes, beginning with a rupture marker.

## Measurement

The model has been operationalized for research through observer-based coding. Researchers developed a new observer-based system for rating confrontation and withdrawal rupture markers and rupture resolution strategies — known as the Rupture Resolution Rating System (3RS).

---

Here's an overview of Eugene Gendlin's Focusing, the felt sense, the Experiencing (EXP) Scale, and the psychotherapy outcome research connecting them:

## Origins in Client-Centered Therapy Research

Focusing grew directly out of a major psychotherapy research project. Experiential Focusing is an outgrowth of a large, highly-regarded psychotherapy research project (Rogers, 1967) where Rogers, Gendlin, and others set out to test the assumptions of client-centered therapy against long-term outcome measures with the population of patients at a state mental hospital. Notably, Carl Rogers and his colleagues, Gendlin among them, were the first who actually listened to audio tapes and tried to analyze and measure psychotherapy process.

The surprising central finding reframed how therapeutic success was understood: success in long-term therapy was already predictable by the fourth session and that the variable was, not so much what the therapist was doing, but what the client was doing. More specifically, clients who came into therapy able to refer to and speak from the fresh, present, bodily-feel of issues and symptoms profited from therapy, almost regardless of what the therapists did. Clients who lacked this capacity for "direct reference" to felt experiencing did not change over time.

Another account emphasizes how striking the predictive power was: from those tapes, they were able to predict very accurately which clients would get better after a year of psychotherapy as determined by certain outcome measures including the client's self-report and the therapist's report. Strikingly, this prediction, based on their experiencing scale, could be made after listening to the very first session. The crucial element was that the important element of positive change had to do with how clients processed their experience internally and was evidenced by the quality of their expression. The clients who got better did so because they could speak from their present/emerging experiencing process: as they spoke they slowed down, became less articulate, and checked their words with how the whole of a situation felt inside their body.

## The Felt Sense

Gendlin distinguished the felt sense from ordinary, recognizable emotions. At High EXP levels, the client refers to the implicit meaning of an event. This is not a speculative attempt to "figure out" or deductively reconstruct probable significance. Nor is it a matter of recognizable emotions, however intense. The implicit significance is spoken of as a concrete, bodily "sense" of a whole situation. Gendlin calls this a felt sense. It is preverbal, a bodily felt whole that is not at first clear.

In his own description of the process, high on the scale, clients can be heard checking what they say against an as yet unclear physically sensed referent we call "felt sense." Importantly, we differentiate the known "gut feeling" (sad, glad, scared) from the as-yet-unclear referent, the "felt sense." A certain kind of attention brings the "felt sense" of a given problem.

## The Experiencing (EXP) Scale

The EXP Scale was created to operationalize and measure this variable. The Experiencing (EXP) Scale measures seven levels of client experiencing. It was designed to measure the extent to which therapy clients refer directly to their immediate experiencing during therapy. They imagined this EXP variable as a continuum, divided into seven levels, with objective third person description at the lowest level, and basic and advanced Focusing at the two highest levels.

The progression through levels works like this: at lower levels, talking is objective and intellectual, while at Middle EXP levels, the client can at least identify some emotions and may also think about events in terms of personal connections, but there is no "focusing" on a felt sense. In a high-EXP process, a client attends directly to this implicit sense and thereby allows its verbal expression. This is a step of therapeutic change. In a Lower EXP level process, a client may fail to discriminate this initially vague sense and get stuck in an intellectual or repetitively emotive process.

The scale is typically scored in two ways: typically, EXP is measured in terms of modal EXP, an index of average observed process, or peak EXP, the upper limit of the client process (Klein et al.).

## Teaching Focusing

A key insight was that this capacity could be deliberately taught rather than treated as a fixed trait. Gendlin devised instructions (Focusing Manual; Gendlin et al., 1968) for teaching just that, which the Experiencing Scale had found correlated with success: attention to an unclear sensed referent. The research suggests this worked: failure-predicted people have now been raised to a success-predicting experiencing level in their therapy (Clarke, 1980).

## Outcome Research Findings

The correlation between EXP and outcome has been replicated extensively. The EXP Scale has been found to be correlated with successful therapy outcome in a number of studies. One summary notes that more than 30 studies now show that a higher experiencing level correlates with more successful therapy (Hendricks, 2002).

The EXP scale is now recognized as one of the most rigorous process measures in the field. It is one of the most studied and validated observational measures in adult psychotherapy research. The scale itself evaluates a client's emotional and cognitive involvement in the therapeutic process. Crucially, the effect holds across different treatment approaches: within the adult literature, across therapeutic orientations, higher EXP is predictive of more successful outcomes.

A notable example compared two very different modalities: Watson and Bedard examined EXP in relation to outcomes in emotion-focused therapy (EFT) and cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) for 40 clients with depression. For both therapeutic approaches, good outcomes were associated with higher modal and peak EXP.

The strongest quantitative evidence comes from meta-analysis: a meta-analysis of 10 studies including 406 clients found that—regardless of treatment focus, approach, or phase—EXP significantly predicted treatment outcomes (r = −.25; Pascual-Leone & Yeryomenko). The authors concluded that depth of emotional experiencing is 'the most promising client process predictor of outcome'.

## Contemporary Use and Methodological Notes

Interestingly, the scale's primary use has migrated to other experiential therapy traditions. The EXP scale was developed in the 1960s as part of the same research that led to Focusing, but in recent years it has been used primarily by researchers interested in Emotion Focused Therapy (EFT) and Process Experiential Therapy (PET).

Researchers have also flagged practical limitations of the seven-level approach. First, the seven level scale requires the rater to make many fine discriminations, which makes it difficult to learn and time-consuming to score. More importantly, because it was impractical to score an entire course of therapy, it became common to score random samples of the therapy, for example three 20 minute periods randomly selected from the beginning, middle, and the end of therapy.
